items.title: 5.4 Determination of Young's modulus of a wire

source_refs.note: Topic 5.4 with Fig. 5.4 (PDF 97-98, printed 94-95). The print reads 'searl apparatus' and 'screw guage'.

blocks.text: Experimentally the magnitude of Young's modulus for a material in the form of a wire can be found with Searle's apparatus (Fig. 5.4). It consists of two wires, an auxiliary or reference wire and a test (experimental) wire, of equal lengths and of the same material and diameter, attached to a rigid support. Both wires are connected to horizontal bars (frames F1 and F2) at the other ends. A constant weight is hung on the hook of the horizontal bar of the reference wire and a hanger on the test wire, so that the wire remains stretched and free from kinks.

blocks.alt: Two long wires hang from a rigid support. The reference wire carries a constant weight; the test wire carries a hanger with slotted weights. Frames on the wires are joined by a spirit level, and a micrometer screw on the test-wire frame measures how far it stretches. A box explains: add load, relevel with the micrometer, read delta L, and Y = (F / A) / (delta L / L).
blocks.caption: Searle's apparatus for Young's modulus (original diagram after Figure 5.4).

items: Measure the initial length L0 of the wire using a metre scale.
Measure the diameter d of the wire using a screw gauge; measure it at several different points along the wire and take the average.
Adjust the spirit level to the horizontal position by turning the micrometer; record the micrometer reading as the reference reading.
Load the test wire with a further weight; the spirit level tilts because of the elongation of the test wire.
Adjust the micrometer screw to restore the spirit level to the horizontal position; subtract the first micrometer reading from the second to obtain the extension of the test wire.
Calculate stress and strain: stress = weight / area of wire = F / A = mg / (pi r^2); strain = delta L / L0 = change in length / original length.
Repeat the above steps by increasing the load on the test wire to obtain more values of stress and strain.
Plot these values on a stress-strain graph; it should be a straight line. Determine the slope Y; the slope equals Young's modulus of the wire.

blocks.prompt: Why are two wires of the same material used, and why is the extension taken from the micrometer rather than by measuring the wire's length directly?
blocks.explanation: The reference wire undergoes the same thermal expansion and the same sag of the support as the test wire, so comparing the two cancels those effects and only the extension due to the added load remains. The extension is a fraction of a millimetre, far below what a metre scale can resolve, whereas the micrometer reads to 0.01 mm.

items: Searle's apparatus: reference and test wires of one material and diameter on a rigid support, frames with a spirit level and a micrometer. Measure L0 (metre scale) and d (screw gauge, averaged); level and read; load, relevel, read: extension; stress = mg/(pi r^2), strain = delta L/L0; repeat; slope of the stress-strain line = Y.
